title: Interactive kernel latency surface mapping and lab protocol
author: Aisha Kapoor
content:
Title: Interactive kernel latency surface mapping and lab protocol

Overview
This document defines the lab protocol, tooling, and interpretation guide for interactive kernel latency surface mapping — a repeatable experiment to discover how scheduler decisions, kernel selection, and request shapes interact to produce the observed latency surface across our GPU fleet. The goal is to produce a compact, actionable artifact (the latency surface) for: triage, kernel hinting, scheduler tuning, and CI gating for kernel rollouts.

Why we need this playbook
- Compliments static microbenchmarks by exposing cross-layer effects (scheduling, batching, KV cache warmup, and transport).
- Produces a 2D/3D surface (example axes: concurrency x sequence length x kernel variant) that helps quantify non-linear tail behavior.
- Provides reproducible artifacts to attach to incident reviews and perf regression PRs.

Scope and assumptions
- Scope: production-like runtime and staging clusters only. Not intended for developer sandbox machines.
- Assumes trace-captured workload shapes (sequence length distribution, token rate, concurrency histogram).
- Requires telemetry stack: tracing enabled, kernel-hint annotations (k_hint), scheduler decisions logged, and KV cache hit-rate metrics.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/perf (on-call: Michael Chen)
- Kernel scheduling lead: Lena Ortiz
- SRE contact for fleet experiments: Tomás Rivera

Definitions
- Latency surface: a vectorized map of p50/p90/p99 generation latency over discretized axes (concurrency, sequence length, kernel variant, model shard count).
- Kernel variant: a named execution path (e.g., fast-attn-v2-fp16, sharded-kv-quant-8b).

High-level experiment steps
1) Select workload corpus
   - Use recent 7-day trace that matches the target customer profile. Export as request-surface.json following the format in Appendix A.
2) Provision experiment cluster
   - Create an isolated staging fleet subset (min size 8 GPUs, matching target hardware generation). Ensure same networking path as prod (VPC peering).
3) Apply instrumentation and deterministic seed
   - Enable full tracing (trace-level=debug), kernel hinting annotations, and set kvcache-deterministic=true for warmup runs.
4) Define axis grid
   - Concurrency: [1, 4, 8, 16, 32]
   - Sequence length: [8, 32, 128, 512]
   - Kernel variants: select 3–4 candidates under test
   - For heterogeneous pools, include shard counts [1, 2, 4]
5) Run warmup phase (10 minutes per grid point)
6) Execute measurement phase (3–10 minutes per grid point depending on noise)
7) Aggregate and synthesize the latency surface
8) Produce findings and suggested action items (kernel hints, scheduler policy changes, rollout gates)

Detailed commands and examples
- Provisioning (example using infra-tool):
  infra-tool create-experiment --name latency-surface-2027-11 --region us-west2 --gpus 8 --image runtime-experiment:v2027.03

- Trace replay command (local runner):
  trace-runner --input request-surface.json --concurrency 8 --sequence-length 128 --interval 0.01 --target http://staging-runtime:8080/generate --annotations k_hint=on

- Kernel probe invocation (on-node):
  sudo /opt/runtime/bin/kernel-probe --pid $RUNTIME_PID --duration 120 --out /tmp/kprobe.json

- Telemetry collection snippets (yaml):
  telemetry_capture: |
    capture: true
    metrics: ["latency_ms.p50","latency_ms.p90","latency_ms.p99","kvcache.hit_rate","kernel.exec_ns"]
    trace: true

Measurement considerations and guardrails
- Warmup is mandatory: discard first 120s of samples per grid point to avoid startup noise.
- Target request-rate should be bounded to avoid saturation outside interest range. Use rate limiter parameter to shape inputs.
- If node-level CPU steals or OOMs are observed, mark grid point as invalid and rerun after fixing interference.
- Use p99 over sliding window of 60s as primary tail metric.

Data model and artifact format
- Latency surface artifact is a newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) file where each record has flat fields only:
  - timestamp, axis_concurrency, axis_sequence_length, kernel_variant, p50_ms, p90_ms, p99_ms, sample_count, kvcache_hit_rate, scheduler_decision
- Attach raw traces (zip) and kernel-probe outputs to the artifact bundle for deep dive.

Interpreting the surface: quick heuristics
- Sharp upward slope in p99 when going from concurrency 8 -> 16 suggests scheduler admission/backpressure tuning required.
- Diverging p90 vs p99 for the same kernel variant indicates tail amplification (likely inter-batch interference).
- If a kernel variant shows better p50 but worse p99 consistently, consider local hedging or slot reservation policies for latency-sensitive tenants.

Recommended actions matrix
| Symptom | Likely cause | Recommended quick action | Longer-term remediation | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| p99 spike at medium concurrency | Kernel blocking on NVLINK or serialization | Enable per-request kernel timeout / hedge | Patch kernel to reduce global locks; add preemption hints | Kernel team |
| p50 improves but p99 worsens | Inter-batch head-of-line contention | Add burst isolation for small sequences | Scheduler crediting by sequence-length class | Scheduler team |
| p99 increases with shard count | KV cache warmup inefficiency | Increase prefetch window for multi-shard requests | Rework KV prefetch algorithm to prioritize hot prefixes | Runtime team |

CI gates and rollout criteria
- Attach latency-surface artifact and p99 delta plots to every kernel rollout PR.
- Mandatory pass criteria for major kernel releases: p99 delta <= +3% across all grid points for the baseline customer corpus, and no grid point with >+10% increase.
- For canary: run abbreviated surface (concurrency [1,8,32], sequence lengths [8,128,512]) in canary fleet with 48h observation window.

Dashboarding and visualization
- Visualize as a 3D surface (concurrency x seq-length x p99) in Grafana using the latency-surface ndjson -> timeseries transformer. Provide a linked panel to sample traces for any selected grid point.
- Store artifacts in object-store prefix: s3://redwood-runtime-experiments/latency-surfaces/{YYYY}/{experiment-id}/artifact.ndjson

Known limitations
- Lab results are sensitive to cross-tenant noise and scheduler tuning; annotate experiments with cluster packing details.
- Results for highly heterogeneous models (different layer shapes) might not be comparable — restrict comparisons to similar model classes.

Reporting template (to attach to PRs/incidents)
- Experiment id: <uuid>
- Date run: <YYYY-MM-DD>
- Cluster: <region>/<flavor>/<k8s-version>
- Workload corpus id: <corpus-id> (link)
- Key findings (bulleted)
- Action items and owners
- Attached artifacts: latency-surface.ndjson, traces.zip, kprobe.json, dashboard-link

Appendix A — request-surface.json example (flattened NDJSON)
{"timestamp":"2027-02-28T14:23:00Z","req_id":"r-123","seq_len":"128","concurrency_bucket":"8","payload_sample":"<redacted>"}

Appendix B — minimal telemetry query examples
- p99 by grid point (promql):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel_variant, seq_len_bucket, concurrency_bucket))

Appendix C — quick trouble-shoot checklist
1) Confirm trace completeness and presence of k_hint annotations.
2) Inspect kernel-probe for long syscall blocking or NVLINK stalls.
3) Check scheduler decision logs for preemptions or admission rejects.
4) Validate KV cache hit rates at grid point; if <60% for expected hot prefixes, rerun with longer warmup.
